title: Al-Fajr: the old cities
hook: 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh built high and went too far (89:6–13)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Fajr, the dawn, and ten nights nobody can quite pin down. Your line was by the dawn.

Every big city has one: the tower built to be the tallest, the name on the side in letters you can read from the highway. And every traveler has stood somewhere else, among broken columns in a desert or a jungle, reading a sign that says a great city stood here, and wondering what the people thought when they built it. Did they think it would last? The second passage of Al-Fajr takes the listener on exactly that kind of tour, through three peoples who built high.
screen: `THE TOWER WITH ITS NAME ON THE SIDE.` → `BROKEN COLUMNS IN THE DESERT.` → `THE OLD CITIES.`

segments.voice: Verse six asks: have you not seen what your Lord did with 'Ad? Then three stops. First, 'Ad, and Iram, the city of pillars, whose like was never made in any land. 'Ad were an ancient Arabian people; their prophet, the Qur'an says elsewhere, was Hud. People have searched for Iram for centuries, and nobody knows for certain where it stood. Second, Thamud, who carved out the rocks in the valley. Their prophet was Salih. Muslims have long connected them with al-Hijr in northwest Arabia, where huge facades are cut into sandstone; archaeologists date those carvings to the Nabataeans, a later people, so the link is tradition, not settled history. Third, Pharaoh, lord of the stakes. Commentators read the stakes as the pegs of great tents or armies, or as monuments fixed firmly in the ground, or as a way he punished people. All three, verse eleven says, overstepped in the land and multiplied corruption. Then, in Pickthall's words: Lo! thy Lord is ever watchful. The Arabic is bil-mirsad, on the lookout, like a watchtower on a road. Here's the irony: these were builders of pillars and towers and monuments, and the real watchtower was never theirs. The Qur'an isn't against building. It's against building as a way of saying I don't answer to anyone. That ends a week: Al-Layl's giver eased toward ease, then the sun, and the soul that can be tended or buried, then the steep path and the two roads, then the dawn. Today, the towers.
screen: `'AD AND IRAM, THE CITY OF PILLARS.` · `THAMUD, WHO CARVED THE ROCK.` · `PHARAOH, LORD OF THE STAKES.` · `YOUR LORD IS ON THE WATCHTOWER.` · then, large: `TOWERS FALL.`

segments.voice: Think of something built to impress: a skyscraper, a stadium, a mansion online, or something of your own, a resume, a profile, a car. Picture it a thousand years from now, sand, grass, a sign for tourists. Without gloom, notice what would still matter about the people who lived there.
Al-Fajr. The dawn, Surah eighty-nine, which walks past 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh, and says your Lord is ever watchful. Today's word.
Your line: towers fall. The question is what outlasts them. A full week, and day one hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Muslims read the Qur'an's accounts of 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh as lessons about pride and power; many who visit ancient ruins recall these verses and reflect on the peoples who built them.

fork.setup: three peoples built high and overstepped. what does Al-Fajr say right after their stories?
fork.reveal: Lo! thy Lord is ever watchful (89:14): on the watchtower, bil-mirsad. the builders of towers were never the ones watching.

original.note: Arabic: "Iram of the pillars," the city of 'Ad (Qur'an 89:7); its location is unknown.

trapdoor: what you thought: old stories about cities that were destroyed.
what it means: three peoples who built high and overstepped, and the reminder that the Lord is on the watch.

what a scholar hears: dhu al-awtad, lord of the stakes, has at least three readings in tafsir; al-Hijr's facades are Nabataean, first century BCE to CE, while Thamud is attested in older Assyrian records.
